criteria.remark: Two images, one on each of two pages, offer no text alternative: the home page hero graphic and the avatar image on the account page carry no alternative text and no other accessible name, so a screen reader announces nothing where they appear and whatever they convey is unavailable to someone who cannot see them. Readers should treat these as two confirmed points where image content is lost, and ask how images are given alternatives across the rest of the product.

Sixteen in-page links across five pages point to a destination that is not there: the header skip link on the home and apply pages aims at "main-content", and links in a home page list aim at "news", but after the link is activated no element on the page has that id or name, so focus does not move anywhere. What was measured is where focus went after activation. A person has to decide whether another mechanism bypasses the same blocks — a heading, a landmark or a collapsible block. skip-link-works could not look on 1 of 37 scans (the path is replayed once for each rule, and this rule needed its end loaded again); what it would have found is not shown.

Eighteen links across six pages have no text a screen reader can announce. Each is an icon-only link — the social media links in the page footer, for example, pointing to external benefits pages — whose only content is a decorative graphic hidden from assistive technology, with no label supplied any other way. Someone using a screen reader reaches these links in the keyboard order and hears nothing identifying where they lead, so the purpose of the link cannot be determined from the link or its surroundings.

Twenty elements across six pages give assistive technology no name. Most are icon-only links, such as the footer social media links whose only content is a graphic hidden from screen readers; the apply form also contains a Social Security number field with no visible or programmatic label, and dropdowns were flagged for the same reason. A screen reader can tell the user a control is present but not what it is for, which affects both reading and completing the form.

Three pieces of text across three pages are too faint to meet the minimum contrast threshold: the amber "Pending" status badge on the status, upload status and account pages sits at 2.27:1 against its white background, where 4.5:1 is required at that size and weight. Readers with low vision, or anyone on a glare-prone screen, may not be able to read the status word that tells them where their application stands. axe could not decide 1 element under this criterion (covered by another element); they are not shown.

Eight form controls across two pages, including the first name, last name, date of birth and Social Security number fields and the household size dropdown on the apply form, draw their keyboard focus indicator as an amber outline measured at 1.66:1 against the white surface behind it, below the 3:1 threshold for such visual indicators. That contrast ratio is what was measured. A person has to decide whether another visual cue identifies the focus.
